unit.title: Serve, Return, Two Bounces
unit.summary: Legal serves (volley and drop), where it must land, return, the two-bounce rule.

lessons.title: Underhand, diagonal, behind the line
lessons.objective: Describe a legal serve position and target.

payload.prompt: Tap the correct target service box for a serve from the right side.

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court. A player stands behind the near baseline on the right side of the centerline, ready to serve.

hotspots.label: Far box on the left of the screen
Far box on the right of the screen
Near box on the left of the screen
Near box on the right of the screen

explanation.correct: Serving from the right, you aim diagonally across the net, into the far box on the opposite side of the centerline. The receiver stands in their own right-hand box, which looks like the left on screen.
explanation.incorrect: A serve never goes straight ahead. It crosses the net diagonally into the box opposite yours, and it has to clear the kitchen.

payload.prompt: Your toe is on the baseline as you hit the serve.

scene.alt: You stand with a toe on the baseline at the moment you hit the serve.

explanation.correct: Foot fault. At the moment you hit the serve, your feet must be behind the baseline, not touching it or the court.
explanation.incorrect: The baseline counts as court for the server. A toe on the line at contact is a foot fault. Stepping in after you hit the ball is fine.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot fault, your toe was on the line.

payload.prompt: What makes a volley serve 'underhand'?

options.text: You toss the ball low
You hit it below your waist with an upward swing
You hit it while crouching
You use a slice grip

explanation.correct: For a volley serve, the paddle meets the ball below your waist and the swing travels upward. It is a rule about contact, not a style choice.
explanation.incorrect: Crouching, tossing low or gripping a certain way does not make it underhand. The rule looks at where you contact the ball and which way the paddle is moving.
explanation.sayThisLine: An underhand serve is hit below the waist, swinging up.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I'm on the right side. Do I serve to the right box?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Not straight ahead. Serves go diagonally across to the opposite box.
Yes, straight ahead to the box in front of you.
It depends on the score.
You can pick either box.

payload.translation: Sam is asking where the serve goes. It always crosses the net diagonally, from the side you are standing on into the box opposite it.

followUps.line: I think it goes diagonally across, not straight ahead. Want to try a couple?
followUps.why: Shares what you know and invites Sam to practice together.

followUps.line: Diagonal, I'm pretty sure. Corner to corner, into the box across the net.
followUps.why: Short and memorable, and honest about how sure you are.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Diagonal serving is one of the clearest rules, so you can say it confidently. Offer it as a friend, not as the rules committee.

lessons.title: The volley serve, in detail
lessons.objective: State the three volley-serve requirements incl. 2026 'clearly'.

payload.prompt: Which is a legal volley serve requirement?

options.text: The paddle head must be above the wrist
Contact must be below the waist with an upward arc
The serve can be hit overhand
The ball must bounce before you hit it

explanation.correct: A volley serve has three requirements: paddle head not above the wrist, contact below the waist, and an upward arc. The 2026 rulebook says each must be clear.
explanation.incorrect: A volley serve is hit before the ball bounces, with a low, upward swing and the paddle head not above the wrist. Overhand is never legal, and a bounce first is the drop serve, which is a different serve.
explanation.sayThisLine: A volley serve is below the waist, swinging up, paddle head not above the wrist.

payload.prompt: Complete the volley-serve rule.
payload.template: On a volley serve the paddle head must not be {{wrist}} the wrist, contact must be {{waist}} the waist, and the arc must be {{arc}}.

explanation.correct: Paddle head not above the wrist, contact below the waist, upward arc. All three have to hold or the serve is a fault.
explanation.incorrect: These three rules keep the serve low and controlled: no overhead slam, paddle head level with or below the wrist, and a swing that travels upward.
explanation.sayThisLine: Below the wrist, below the waist, moving up.

payload.prompt: Put one volley serve in order.

items.text: Server calls the score out loud
items.why: The server announces the score before serving so everyone agrees on it.

items.text: Server sets up behind the baseline
items.why: Feet stay behind the baseline until the ball is struck.

items.text: Server swings low and upward, contact below the waist
items.why: This is the moment the three volley-serve requirements are judged.

items.text: Ball clears the kitchen and lands in the diagonal box
items.why: The serve only counts if it clears the net and kitchen, including its line, and lands in the box.

explanation.correct: Call the score, set up behind the baseline, serve with a low upward swing, and watch it land past the kitchen in the diagonal box.
explanation.incorrect: A serve runs in this order: call the score, set up, swing, land. The swing is judged at contact, and the landing is judged last.
explanation.sayThisLine: Call the score, set up behind the line, swing low, land it past the kitchen.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: My serve looked okay, but they called it a fault.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Did they say why? If it isn't clearly legal, it can be called.
That's just bad officiating.
You probably stepped over the line.
Don't worry about it.

payload.translation: The 2026 rulebook asks that the paddle position, contact height and upward arc all be clear. In officiated play, a serve that is not clearly legal can be faulted.

followUps.line: Did they say which part? I've heard borderline ones can be called when an official is watching.
followUps.why: Asks a specific question and is honest about what you know.

followUps.line: Could be the paddle position or the contact height. Want to film one and look together?
followUps.why: Offers help without claiming to have seen the fault.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You did not see the serve, so do not diagnose it. Ask what they called and listen.

lessons.title: The drop serve
lessons.objective: Explain why the drop serve is allowed at any height and what changes.

payload.prompt: What is the key difference with a drop serve?

options.text: You can hit it from any height, as long as it bounced first
You toss it up first, then let it bounce
It doesn't count on the first try
You may serve from inside the baseline

explanation.correct: For a drop serve you let go of the ball (no toss or push), let it bounce, then hit it. Because it bounced first, the waist and upward-arc limits of the volley serve do not apply.
explanation.incorrect: The drop serve keeps the same landing rules (diagonal, in the box, past the kitchen) and the same spot behind the baseline. The difference is the bounce, which frees up your swing height.
explanation.sayThisLine: With a drop serve the ball bounces first, so contact height is up to you.

payload.prompt: Which serve style is the best starting point?

situation.narrative: You're learning to serve and you have to pick a style.

facts.label: Volley serve
facts.value: Hit before it bounces, low with an upward swing.

facts.label: Drop serve
facts.value: Let go, let it bounce, then hit it. Many find it easier.

facts.label: Outcome
facts.value: Both land in the same box and count the same.

options.label: Start with drop serve; easier mechanics to master
options.consequence: Drop serve removes one layer of complexity so you can focus on aim and landing. Volley serve comes later when you're confident.
considerations: Same landing rules as volley serve
You can always learn volley later

options.label: Learn the volley serve first, it looks more advanced
options.consequence: Ambitious, and perfectly legal. Plenty of strong players use the volley serve, but it has more rules to hit cleanly, so it can be a frustrating first step.
considerations: Three contact rules to get right at once
Worth learning, just not required first
Can add it later when you want

payload.expertNote: Both serves are fully legal and respected. A drop serve is a friendly way to get reliable aim and landing first; the volley serve can come later if you want it.
payload.sayThisLine: Drop serve is the shortcut to a reliable serve.

payload.prompt: You drop the ball and it bounces. You step over the baseline, then hit it.

scene.alt: You stand over the baseline after dropping the ball; it is bouncing and you are about to hit it.

explanation.correct: Foot fault. Even on a drop serve, your feet must be behind the baseline until you hit the ball.
explanation.incorrect: The baseline rule applies to both volley and drop serves. Stepping in before contact is a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot fault: you crossed the baseline.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Drop serve is so much easier. I'm just gonna use that.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Smart move. It's a totally valid way to serve.
But the pros use volley serves.
You'll have to learn volley eventually.
Drop serve is cheating.

payload.translation: The drop serve is fully legal and common at every level. If it works for Sam, it works, so there is no pressure to switch.

followUps.line: Drop serve is totally legit. Lots of players stick with it their whole career.
followUps.why: Affirms Sam's choice without false comparisons.

followUps.line: Go for it. Same rules for landing, just easier form.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Do not push Sam toward the volley serve. Enthusiasm beats opinions when you are still learning.

lessons.title: Aim it, land it
lessons.objective: Land a serve in the correct diagonal box past the kitchen line.

payload.prompt: Your serve lands right on the kitchen line on the far side.

scene.alt: Ball marking the kitchen line on the far court.

explanation.correct: Short serve. The kitchen line is part of the kitchen, so landing on it is a fault. You must clear the kitchen line.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen line on a serve is the boundary; landing there is short. It has to be past the line to be good.
explanation.sayThisLine: Landing on the kitchen line is a short serve.

payload.prompt: Your serve clips the net cord and lands in the correct service box.

options.text: It's a let, replay the serve
The serve is good, play on
It's a fault
You get to choose

explanation.correct: No service lets in pickleball. A serve that clips the net but lands in is live, and play continues.
explanation.incorrect: Tennis has lets; pickleball does not. Net cord on a serve that lands in? Play on.
explanation.sayThisLine: No service lets. If it clears and lands in, it counts.

payload.prompt: Complete the serve landing rule.
payload.template: A legal serve must land past the kitchen line and within the {{area}}.

explanation.correct: The serve must land in the diagonal service box on the far side, past the kitchen line. Lines are in.
explanation.incorrect: The landing zone is the service box. Anything outside it or in the kitchen is a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Serve must land in the service box, past the kitchen.

lessons.title: Return of serve
lessons.objective: Know the return must bounce and why deep is smart.

payload.prompt: What is the rule about the return of serve?

options.text: You must volley it back
It must bounce on your side before you hit it
You can hit it in the air if you want
There is no return rule

explanation.correct: The return must bounce first (two-bounce rule). You cannot volley the serve; you have to let it land and bounce.
explanation.incorrect: Like the serve, the return is locked by the two-bounce rule. Let it bounce, then hit it.
explanation.sayThisLine: You have to let the return bounce.

payload.prompt: Where should you aim your return?

situation.narrative: The serve lands near the baseline on your side. You can hit it back in two directions.

facts.label: Short return
facts.value: Toward their kitchen, close to the net

facts.label: Deep return
facts.value: Toward their baseline, deep in the court

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: You're at the baseline after receiving the serve

options.label: Hit deep, toward their baseline
options.consequence: A deep return keeps the serving team back at their baseline, which gives your team time to walk up to the kitchen line.
considerations: Buys your team time to advance
Makes their third shot harder to play well

options.label: Hit short, near their kitchen
options.consequence: A short return lets the serving team step forward sooner and gives them an easier ball to work with, while you are still back near your baseline.
considerations: Gives the serving team an easier third shot
Lets them get up toward the kitchen line sooner
A tricky target for most players to hit accurately

payload.expertNote: Going deep is the usual safe choice for a return: it buys your team time to move forward. It is a habit worth knowing, not a law.
payload.sayThisLine: A deep return buys time to get up to the kitchen line.

payload.prompt: The serve is coming. You hit it before it bounces.

scene.alt: The serve is still in the air above your side of the court and you swing at it before it has bounced.

explanation.correct: Fault. The receiving team has to let the serve bounce before hitting it, so this return is a volley and is called against you. This is the first half of the two-bounce rule.
explanation.incorrect: Letting the serve bounce first is required for the receiver, even if the ball looks easy to reach in the air.
explanation.sayThisLine: The serve has to bounce before I return it.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: My returns always land short. They're destroying me on the third shot.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: I've heard deep returns buy time. Want to try aiming for the back line?
That's rough. Keep trying.
Just hit it harder.
Returns aren't that important.

payload.translation: Sam keeps returning the serve short, which gives the serving team an easy third shot. Aiming deep is the usual fix because it keeps them back and buys Sam time to move up.

followUps.line: What do you aim for on the return? I've heard deep gives you time to get forward.
followUps.why: Asks a real question and offers what you know without coaching.

followUps.line: Want to practice a few deep ones together?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Share it as something you have learned, not as a lesson. You are cheering Sam on, not coaching from a notebook.

payload.prompt: Serve and return have both bounced. The next ball is in the air.

scene.alt: You stand behind the kitchen line. The serve and the return have each bounced, and the next ball is coming at you in the air.

explanation.correct: Volley away. Once the serve and the return have each bounced, the two-bounce rule is finished and anyone may hit the ball in the air, as long as they are not in the kitchen.
explanation.incorrect: The bounces are only required for the first two shots. After that, volleys are fair game outside the kitchen.
explanation.sayThisLine: After the serve and return, volleys are fair game.

payload.prompt: Put the opening sequence of a rally in order.

items.text: Serve is hit and bounces on the receiving side
items.why: Every rally starts with a serve, and it must bounce before anyone returns it.

items.text: Receiver hits the return after that bounce
items.why: The receiving team may not volley the serve.

items.text: Return bounces on the serving side
items.why: The serving team must let the return bounce too.

items.text: Serving team hits the third shot, and volleys are now allowed
items.why: Both required bounces are done, so the game opens up.

explanation.correct: Serve bounces, return is hit, return bounces, then the third shot. After those two bounces anyone may volley, outside the kitchen.
explanation.incorrect: The order is locked: the serve bounces, the return is hit, the return bounces, and only then does free play begin.
explanation.sayThisLine: The serve bounces, the return bounces, then it is open play.

payload.prompt: Why does the two-bounce rule exist?

options.text: To slow down the game
To keep the serving team from rushing the net immediately
To make the game fair for beginners
No particular reason

explanation.correct: Because the serving team has to let the return bounce, they cannot charge the net and volley everything right away. That keeps the start of the rally fair.
explanation.incorrect: It is not about beginners or speed. Without the rule, the serving team could rush the net and smash the return, and the receivers would have no chance.
explanation.sayThisLine: The two-bounce rule stops the serving team from rushing the net.

payload.prompt: Complete the two-bounce rule.
payload.template: The {{shot1}} must bounce on the receiving side, the {{shot2}} must bounce on the serving side, then anyone may volley.

explanation.correct: The serve bounces on the receiving side, and the return bounces on the serving side. After those two bounces the game opens up, outside the kitchen.
explanation.incorrect: It is one bounce per side: the serve lands with the receivers, then the return lands with the servers. After that, volleys are allowed.
explanation.sayThisLine: One bounce on each side, then you can volley.

lessons.title: Serve faults, sorted
lessons.objective: Sort serve faults from legal serves; hear 'fault!' and know why.

payload.prompt: Which is NOT a serve fault?

options.text: Stepping over the baseline while serving
Serving overhand
Hitting the ball before it bounces (drop serve)
Clipping the net and landing in the service box

explanation.correct: No service lets: clipping the net and landing in is a good serve, not a fault.
explanation.incorrect: Foot faults, an overhand swing, hitting a drop serve before it bounces, and landing short or out are all faults. A net clip that lands in is not one.
explanation.sayThisLine: Net clip that lands in? It's good.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: They called a fault. Is it just the line calls or is there more to it?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Could be a lot of things: foot fault, wrong box, landing short, overhand motion.
It's usually just the line.
If they called it, it must be right.
Just serve again.

payload.translation: A serve can be faulted for several reasons: a foot fault, landing short in the kitchen, landing in the wrong box or out, or an illegal swing. Help Sam work out which one it was.

followUps.line: Could be a foot on the line, landing short, the wrong box, or the swing. Did they say which?
followUps.why: Names the categories and invites Sam to figure it out.

followUps.line: Serve faults have a bunch of possible reasons. It's worth asking what went wrong.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to diagnose a call you did not see. Helping Sam ask the right question is plenty.

payload.prompt: Match the serve fault to its description.

pairs.definition: Standing on or over the baseline when you serve
Landing in the kitchen or on the kitchen line
Landing in the box straight across from you instead of the diagonal one
Landing outside the baseline or sideline

explanation.summary: Foot faults, short serves, wrong boxes and out-of-bounds serves are the main fault types. Clipping the net and landing in is not a fault, because there are no service lets.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot, short, wrong box, out of bounds: those are serve faults.

payload.title: The serve got called a fault
payload.setting: Sam is frustrated about a serve call.

exchanges.theirMessage: They called my serve a fault. I have no idea why.

replies.text: Did you ask which one? Foot, short, wrong box, or something else?
replies.theirResponse: Oh, good idea. I'll ask next time.
replies.coachNote: You named the categories; that's helpful.
Sympathetic, but a question would help more.

replies.text: Serves don't have that many rules. They probably made it up.
replies.theirResponse: Wow, okay. They're not making it up.
replies.coachNote: Serves have many rules. Don't dismiss the call.

exchanges.theirMessage: What are all the things that make a serve a fault?

replies.text: I'm still learning, but foot fault, landing short in the kitchen, wrong box, out of bounds, or an illegal swing.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, that makes sense. That's a lot.
replies.coachNote: You shared what you know and were honest that you are still learning.

replies.text: A bunch of things. Just try again.
replies.coachNote: Kind, but Sam asked for the list. Even a short one helps.

replies.text: It's whatever they say it is. Don't overthink it.
replies.theirResponse: That doesn't help me get better.
replies.coachNote: Waving it away leaves Sam stuck. Saying 'I'm not sure, let's look it up' would have been fine.

payload.closingNote: A serve fault is usually about your feet, where the ball landed, which box you aimed at, or how you swung. A net clip that lands in is still good. Now you can decode most calls.
